setup:
import numpy as np
import scipy
import scipy.linalg
from scipy import linalg, signal
from scipy.sparse.linalg import cg, eigs
from numpy.random import default_rng
np.set_printoptions(precision=6, suppress=True, linewidth=76, threshold=10000)
small = np.array([[3., 1.], [2., 4.]])
other = np.array([[2., 3.], [5., 2.]])
scan = np.arange(1., 46.).reshape(5, 9)
threshold = np.array([[0.2, 0.7, 0.5], [0.9, 0.4, 0.8]])
complex_matrix = np.array([[1+2j, 3-1j], [2j, 4+0j]])
spd = np.array([[6., 2., 1.], [2., 5., 2.], [1., 2., 4.]])
rect = np.array([[1., 0.], [1., 1.], [1., 2.]])
for name in ['small', 'other', 'scan', 'threshold', 'complex_matrix', 'spd', 'rect']:
    print(name + ' =')
    print(globals()[name])

examples.title: Assemble blocks
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
c, d = np.eye(2), np.zeros((2, 2))
print(np.block([[a, b], [c, d]]))

examples.title: Rows 3 through 21 with a stride of two
Matrix multiplication
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
print(a @ b)

examples.title: Elementwise multiplication
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
print(a * b)

examples.title: Elementwise division
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
print(a / b)

examples.title: Select columns using index positions
examples.code:
a = threshold.copy()
v = np.array([0.3, 0.9, 0.7])
print(a[:, np.nonzero(v > 0.5)[0]])

examples.title: Select columns using a Boolean mask
examples.code:
a = threshold.copy()
v = np.array([0.3, 0.9, 0.7])
print(a[:, v.T > 0.5])
v = v.reshape(-1, 1)
print(a[:, v.ravel() > 0.5])
examples.note: The first call uses a one-dimensional vector. For an actual two-dimensional column vector, ravel() gives a one-dimensional column mask.

examples.title: Multiply by a strict Boolean mask
examples.note: The entry equal to 0.5 becomes zero here. It remains 0.5 in the previous example because that assignment tests a < 0.5.

examples.title: Copy an array
examples.code:
x = small.copy()
y = x.copy()
y[0, 0] = 99
print(y)
print(x)
examples.note: Changing the copy leaves x unchanged.

examples.title: Copy a row
examples.code:
x = small.copy()
y = x[1, :].copy()
y[0] = 99
print(y)
print(x)

examples.title: Flatten an array
examples.code:
x = small.copy()
y = x.flatten()
print(y)
print(x.flatten("F"))
examples.note: The default traversal reads rows first. The F option reads columns first, matching MATLAB linear indexing.

examples.title: Random values with a fixed seed
examples.code:
from numpy.random import default_rng
rng = default_rng(42)
print(rng.random((3, 4)))
from numpy import random
random.seed(42)
try:
    random.rand((3, 4))
except TypeError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__ + ": " + str(error))
print(random.rand(3, 4))
examples.note: The older call in the table passes a tuple to rand, which expects separate dimension arguments. The corrected call is random.rand(3, 4). The two generators use different random streams.

examples.title: Dense coordinate grids
examples.note: mgrid returns arrays shaped (9, 6); meshgrid uses (6, 9) with its default xy indexing.

examples.title: Open coordinate grids
examples.note: The table omits the closing parenthesis in its ix_ call. The calls here include the np namespace and the missing parenthesis.

examples.title: Repeat a matrix
examples.code:
a = small.copy()
m, n = 2, 3
print(np.tile(a, (m, n)))

examples.title: Join columns
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
print(np.concatenate((a, b), 1))
print(np.hstack((a, b)))
print(np.column_stack((a, b)))
print(np.c_[a, b])

examples.title: Join rows
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
print(np.concatenate((a, b)))
print(np.vstack((a, b)))
print(np.r_[a, b])

examples.title: Maximum over all entries
examples.code:
a = small.copy()
print(a.max())
print(np.nanmax(a))
a[0, 0] = np.nan
print(a.max())
print(np.nanmax(a))
examples.note: nanmax ignores the inserted NaN, while max propagates it.

examples.title: Elementwise maximum
examples.code:
a, b = small.copy(), other.copy()
print(np.maximum(a, b))

examples.title: Logical AND
examples.code:
a = np.array([0, 2, 3, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0])
print(np.logical_and(a, b))

examples.title: Logical OR
examples.code:
a = np.array([0, 2, 3, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0])
print(np.logical_or(a, b))

examples.title: Bitwise AND
examples.code:
a = np.array([0, 2, 3, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0])
print(a & b)

examples.title: Bitwise OR
examples.code:
a = np.array([0, 2, 3, 0])
b = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0])
print(a | b)

examples.title: Square and rectangular linear systems
examples.code:
a = spd.copy()
b = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
print(linalg.solve(a, b))
a = rect.copy()
b = np.array([1., 2., 2.])
print(linalg.lstsq(a, b))
examples.note: lstsq returns the solution, residual sum of squares, rank, and singular values.

examples.title: A system with the unknown on the left
examples.code:
a = small.copy()
b = np.array([[1., 2.], [4., 3.]])
x = linalg.solve(a.T, b.T).T
print(x)
print(x @ a)
examples.note: Transposing x a = b gives a.T x.T = b.T.

examples.title: Singular value decomposition
examples.code:
a = rect.copy()
U, S, Vh = linalg.svd(a)
V = Vh.T
print(U)
print(S)
print(V)
examples.note: The inputs are real, so Vh.T gives V. A complex input would require Vh.conj().T.

examples.title: Cholesky factorization
examples.note: SciPy returns an upper triangular factor by default, so a = U.T @ U for this real matrix.

examples.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
examples.code:
a = spd.copy()
D, V = linalg.eig(a)
print(D)
print(V)

examples.title: Generalized eigenvalues
examples.code:
a = spd.copy()
b = np.diag([1., 2., 3.])
D, V = linalg.eig(a, b)
print(D)
print(V)
examples.note: Each column v satisfies a @ v = lambda * b @ v.

examples.title: Three eigenpairs of a larger matrix
examples.code:
a = np.diag([2., 3., 5., 7., 11., 13.])
D, V = eigs(a, k=3, v0=np.ones(6))
print(D)
print(V)
examples.note: The fixed starting vector makes the iterative calculation reproducible. The three largest magnitudes are 13, 11, and 7.

examples.title: QR factorization
examples.code:
a = rect.copy()
Q, R = linalg.qr(a)
print(Q)
print(R)
Q, R = linalg.qr(a, mode="economic")
print(Q)
print(R)
examples.note: The first call runs the table entry. The economic form also matches the dimensions requested by MATLAB qr(a, 0).

examples.title: LU factorization
examples.code:
a = small.copy()
P, L, U = linalg.lu(a)
print(P)
print(L)
print(U)
print(P @ L @ U)
examples.note: SciPy uses a = P @ L @ U.

examples.title: Conjugate gradients
examples.code:
a = spd.copy()
b = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
x, info = cg(a, b, rtol=1e-12, atol=0.0)
print(x)
print(info)
examples.note: The matrix is symmetric positive definite. A status of zero indicates convergence.

examples.title: Default sorting and column sorting
examples.note: The table lists these as alternatives, but np.sort(a) sorts along the last axis by default. The in-place axis=0 call sorts each column.

examples.title: Sort each row
examples.code:
a = small.copy()
print(np.sort(a, axis=1))
a.sort(axis=1)
print(a)

examples.title: Sort rows by their first entry
examples.code:
a = np.array([[3., 1.], [1., 4.], [2., 0.]])
I = np.argsort(a[:, 0])
b = a[I, :]
print(I)
print(b)

examples.title: Linear regression
examples.code:
Z = rect.copy()
y = np.array([1., 2., 2.])
x = linalg.lstsq(Z, y)
print(x)
print(Z @ x[0])
examples.note: The fitted line has intercept 7/6 and slope 1/2. The first item of the returned tuple contains those coefficients.

examples.title: Fourier resampling
examples.code:
t = np.arange(12.) / 12
x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)
q = 3
try:
    signal.resample(x, np.ceil(len(x)/q))
except TypeError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__ + ": " + str(error))
print(signal.resample(x, int(np.ceil(len(x)/q))))
examples.note: resample requires an integer output length. It uses Fourier resampling and assumes periodic input; it is not the same filtering algorithm as decimate.
